steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the section on the broadcast incentive auction for an encyclopedia article on the 2016 United States wireless spectrum auction, following it from the FCC's rules and the disputes over them through each stage of bidding to the final results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- How the reverse and forward auctions were meant to work
- FCC guidelines and rules (2014–2015) and objections
- Filing window, opening prices and clearing targets
- LPTV stations and the court challenge
- The bidding stages and falling targets
- Final results and winning bidders

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Overview
  - reverse + forward auctions to repack TV stations, free spectrum for wireless
  - phases, targets for spectrum reallocated, forward proceeds must pay for reverse auction + transition costs
- Guidelines, April 18, 2014
  - stations keep coverage area as of February 22, 2012 if possible
  - Channel 37 = "guard band" between broadcasting and wireless
  - deadlines for upgrades; all done after 39 months; Wheeler: missing deadline not necessarily off the air
  - framework approved 3-2; NAB: commission failed to compensate broadcasters / guarantee service
- 2015 rules
  - July 2, 2015 filing, EOBC (over a hundred TV stations): population data too important, $8.3 billion drop in opening prices without "relatively minor" changes; reverse auction so these are highest possible prices
  - July 16: FCC to finalize rules; move to new channels 39 months after auction; no reserved channel for noncommercial broadcasters
  - procedures vote moved to August 6; auction set for March 29, 2016
  - after vote: Ajit Pai, too many broadcasters "placed in the wireless band" -> interference
  - Dennis Wharton (NAB EVP communications): minimized payments, interference, "a handout of free spectrum with no public interest obligations to multibillion dollar companies", hurts local news, LPTV, translators
  - LPTV Spectrum Coalition, CTIA objected; EOBC: no one happy but compromise enough
  - NAB petitions: don't penalize non-participants; don't move stations to duplex gap
- Filing window and prices
  - October 15 Applications Procedure Public Notice: noon December 1 to 6 pm December 18 (later December 8 to January 12)
  - no new stations after; bids not final until March 29, 2016
  - opening bid prices October 16; three categories: give up/share channel (full price), UHF to high VHF (less), high VHF to low VHF (lower, not lowest); also people served, interference
- Clearing target
  - Auction 1001; aim 144 MHz for resale to wireless
  - 144 met -> channels up to 26; minimum 42 MHz -> up to 44
  - if missed, lower target, repeat until reached
  - one vacant channel per market for unlicensed devices
  - target announced: 126 MHz
- LPTV
  - fewer channels for relocation, not protected after; thousands to be relocated
  - not allowed to participate, could lose spectrum
  - May 5: Scott Caulkins (Caulkins & Bruce PC), DC Circuit: Spectrum Act gives LPTV "essentially the same [spectrum] rights"; secondary only if causing interference, repacking -> more interference
  - FCC attorney Jacob Lewis: LPTV secondary, else too many to relocate
- Bidding
  - bidders must bid on 95 percent of census blocks where interest shown
  - August: Comcast, AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon, others; 100 MHz; over $11 billion; goal $88.4 billion
  - stage one ended after two weeks, only $22.45 billion
  - stage two target 114 MHz, goal $54.6 billion, two channels per market; less spectrum -> lower costs
  - further failure: 108 MHz (one channel per market); stage three fails -> 84 MHz, additional four channels per market
  - lower target -> less paid to stations, fewer public stations; public stations not "repacked" pay own upgrades
  - stage two ended October 19, $21.5 billion, $33.1 billion short
  - reverse stage three began November 1, 108 MHz
  - paired blocks per market 10 -> 9 -> 8; four impaired blocks (interference in less than 15 percent of area) protected Mexican channels below 37; two markets 15 to 50 percent
  - forward stage three began December 5; $40.3 billion for 108 MHz
  - reverse stage four ended January 13, 2017; $10.05 billion for 84 MHz, seven licenses per market
  - 70 MHz to wireless, 14 MHz unlicensed; fewer stations move, none in buffer or wireless bands
- Results
  - bidding ended March 30; April 12 FCC announced completion
  - raised $19.8 billion; more spectrum for faster 5G
  - nearly $10.1 billion to 175 TV stations, $7.3 billion to Treasury, $1.8 billion for repacking
  - Lawrence Chu (FCC advisor): success, "there will be some people disappointed on the broadcaster side."
  - T-Mobile almost $8 billion, 1,525 licenses, 45 percent of low-band, whole-country coverage, about four times its spectrum
  - Dish $6.2 billion, 486 licenses; Comcast 73 licenses, $1.7 billion; AT&T $910 million, 23 licenses; U.S. Cellular $328.6 million, 188 licenses

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The reverse and forward auctions would be done in several phases, to repack TV stations and free up spectrum for wireless communications. There would be targets for how much spectrum would be reallocated, and the payments had to balance, so that the proceeds from the forward auction paid for the reverse auction plus the transition costs.

The FCC announced guidelines for the auction on April 18, 2014. All stations would keep their coverage area as of February 22, 2012, if this was possible. Channel 37 would become a "guard band" between broadcasting and wireless services. Each station would get a deadline to make its upgrades, and all stations were expected to complete the transition after 39 months. Wheeler said later that if stations could not meet the deadline they would not necessarily have to go off the air. The FCC approved the framework 3-2, and the NAB claimed the commission had not met its obligation to compensate broadcasters and guarantee service for viewers.

The Expanding Opportunities for Broadcasters Coalition (EOBC), which represented over a hundred TV stations that were planning to participate in the incentive auction, said in a July 2, 2015 filing that population data was too important and could cause an $8.3 billion drop in opening prices unless "relatively minor" changes were made. Because the incentive auction was a reverse auction, even these prices were the highest possible. On July 16, the FCC planned to make the rules of the auction final, including requiring stations to move to their new channels 39 months after the auction, and not having a reserved channel for noncommercial broadcasters. The vote on procedures was moved to August 6, but the auction was set for March 29, 2016.

After the vote, FCC commissioner Ajit Pai said that the plan "permits too many broadcasters to be placed in the wireless band", and this would result in interference between TV stations and others using the band. Dennis Wharton, who is NAB executive vice president of communications, said that the vote minimized what stations would receive for giving up broadcasting and guaranteed numerous interference problems, and that it gave "a handout of free spectrum with no public interest obligations to multibillion dollar companies" while it hurt local television news and especially LPTV stations and translators. The LPTV Spectrum Coalition and CTIA objected to the vote, and the EOBC said that no one would be happy but the compromise would be enough.

The NAB filed petitions that asked the FCC not to penalize stations that did not participate in the auction, and that asked for stations not to be moved to the duplex gap.

On October 15, the Applications Procedure Public Notice set the filing window as noon December 1 through 6 pm December 18, which was later changed to December 8 through January 12. After that no more stations could join, but the bids from the ones that did would not be final until March 29, 2016. On October 16 the FCC released the opening bid prices. There were three categories: stations giving up or sharing channels, which would mean offering the full price, stations moving from UHF to high VHF, which was less than full price, and stations moving from high VHF to low VHF, which was lower than full price but not the lowest. The number of people served and interference were other factors.

- Clearing target
  - Auction 1001, aim 144 MHz for resale to wireless; 144 -> channels up to 26; minimum 42 MHz -> up to 44
  - if "clearing target" not met, lower target, continue until reached
  - one vacant channel per market for unlicensed devices
  - announced target: 126 MHz
- LPTV
  - fewer relocation channels, not protected; thousands to relocate; not allowed to participate, could lose spectrum
  - May 5, Scott Caulkins (Caulkins & Bruce PC), DC Circuit Court: "essentially the same [spectrum] rights" as full-power; secondary only if causing interference
  - FCC attorney Jacob Lewis: secondary, otherwise too many stations to relocate
- Bidding stages
  - bid on 95 percent of census blocks with interest
  - August: Comcast, AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon and others, 100 MHz, over $11 billion, goal $88.4 billion
  - stage one ended after two weeks at $22.45 billion
  - stage two: 114 MHz, goal $54.6 billion (two channels per market); next 108 MHz (one channel), then 84 MHz (additional four channels)
  - lower target -> less to stations, fewer public stations; public stations not "repacked" pay own upgrades
  - stage two ended October 19: $21.5 billion, $33.1 billion short; reverse stage three November 1, 108 MHz
  - paired blocks 10, 9, 8; four impaired blocks (<15 percent) protect Mexican channels below 37; two markets 15 to 50 percent
  - forward stage three December 5, $40.3 billion for 108 MHz
  - reverse stage four ended January 13, 2017: $10.05 billion, 84 MHz, seven licenses per market; 70 MHz wireless, 14 MHz unlicensed; none in buffer or wireless bands
- Results
  - bidding ended March 30; completion announced April 12
  - $19.8 billion, 5G; nearly $10.1 billion to 175 stations, $7.3 billion Treasury, $1.8 billion repacking
  - Lawrence Chu: success, "there will be some people disappointed on the broadcaster side."
  - T-Mobile almost $8 billion, 1,525 licenses, 45 percent low-band; Dish $6.2 billion, 486; Comcast 73 for $1.7 billion; AT&T $910 million, 23; U.S. Cellular $328.6 million, 188

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The reverse and forward auctions would be done in several phases, to repack TV stations and free up spectrum for wireless communications. There would be targets for how much spectrum would be reallocated, and the payments had to balance, so that the proceeds from the forward auction paid for the reverse auction plus the transition costs.

The FCC announced guidelines for the auction on April 18, 2014. All stations would keep their coverage area as of February 22, 2012, if this was possible. Channel 37 would become a "guard band" between broadcasting and wireless services. Each station would get a deadline to make its upgrades, and all stations were expected to complete the transition after 39 months. Wheeler said later that if stations could not meet the deadline they would not necessarily have to go off the air. The FCC approved the framework 3-2, and the NAB claimed the commission had not met its obligation to compensate broadcasters and guarantee service for viewers.

The Expanding Opportunities for Broadcasters Coalition (EOBC), which represented over a hundred TV stations that were planning to participate in the incentive auction, said in a July 2, 2015 filing that population data was too important and could cause an $8.3 billion drop in opening prices unless "relatively minor" changes were made. Because the incentive auction was a reverse auction, even these prices were the highest possible. On July 16, the FCC planned to make the rules of the auction final, including requiring stations to move to their new channels 39 months after the auction, and not having a reserved channel for noncommercial broadcasters. The vote on procedures was moved to August 6, but the auction was set for March 29, 2016.

After the vote, FCC commissioner Ajit Pai said that the plan "permits too many broadcasters to be placed in the wireless band", and this would result in interference between TV stations and others using the band. Dennis Wharton, who is NAB executive vice president of communications, said that the vote minimized what stations would receive for giving up broadcasting and guaranteed numerous interference problems, and that it gave "a handout of free spectrum with no public interest obligations to multibillion dollar companies" while it hurt local television news and especially LPTV stations and translators. The LPTV Spectrum Coalition and CTIA objected to the vote, and the EOBC said that no one would be happy but the compromise would be enough.

The NAB filed petitions that asked the FCC not to penalize stations that did not participate in the auction, and that asked for stations not to be moved to the duplex gap.

On October 15, the Applications Procedure Public Notice set the filing window as noon December 1 through 6 pm December 18, which was later changed to December 8 through January 12. After that no more stations could join, but the bids from the ones that did would not be final until March 29, 2016. On October 16 the FCC released the opening bid prices. There were three categories: stations giving up or sharing channels, which would mean offering the full price, stations moving from UHF to high VHF, which was less than full price, and stations moving from high VHF to low VHF, which was lower than full price but not the lowest. The number of people served and interference were other factors.

The FCC designated the auction as Auction 1001, and its purpose was to make 144 MHz available for resale to wireless companies. If this target was met, broadcasters would have been repacked into channels up to 26. If only the minimum target of 42 MHz was met, channels up to 44 would have been used. It was possible the "clearing target" would not be met, and then a lower target would have been set, and the process would continue until a target was reached. In each market where there are still vacant channels, the FCC intends one of them to be used for unlicensed devices.

The FCC announced that the clearing target would be 126 MHz. This meant there were fewer channels for relocating LPTV stations, and these would not be protected after the auction. It was believed that thousands of LPTV stations would have to be relocated. LPTV stations argued that they could lose spectrum because they were not allowed to participate in the process. On May 5, Scott Caulkins of Caulkins & Bruce PC, who represented one of the owners of LPTV stations, argued before the DC Circuit Court that the Spectrum Act and FCC authority gave LPTV stations "essentially the same [spectrum] rights" as full-power stations. He said they could only be considered secondary if they caused interference, but the result of repacking would be more interference. FCC attorney Jacob Lewis said that LPTV stations would be secondary and that considering their rights would mean too many stations had to be relocated.

In the forward auction each bidder was required to bid on 95 percent of the census blocks where an interest was shown. As of August, Comcast, AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon and others had submitted bids in the forward auction for 100 MHz of spectrum, totaling over $11 billion, and the goal was $88.4 billion.

When the FCC ended stage one of the forward auction after two weeks, only $22.45 billion had been raised. After the second stage of the reverse auction, the target for stage two of the forward auction was 114 MHz, and the desired goal was $54.6 billion, which was enough for two channels per market. Since there was less spectrum to be purchased, lower demand could mean lower costs for the wireless providers. If stage two failed the target could be reduced further, to 108 MHz, or one channel per market. If stage three also failed, the target could even be 84 MHz, which would be an additional four channels per market. The lower the target was, the lower the amount paid to stations, but also the fewer public stations that could participate. And public stations that are not "repacked" have to pay for their own equipment upgrades.

Stage two of the forward auction ended October 19 with $21.5 billion in total bids, which was $33.1 billion less than expected. The third stage of the reverse auction began November 1 with a target of 108 MHz. The number of paired blocks per market was 10 at the start, then 9 in stage two, and 8 in stage three. Four impaired blocks, which had interference in less than 15 percent of an area, protected Mexican channels below 37. Two markets had interference in 15 to 50 percent of an area.

Stage three of the forward auction began December 5, after the total bids for stage three were $40.3 billion for 108 MHz. Stage four of the reverse auction ended January 13, 2017 with $10.05 billion paid for 84 MHz, which is seven licenses in each market. Of that, 70 MHz goes to the wireless companies and 14 MHz is for unlicensed use. Because less spectrum was cleared, fewer stations will move and none will be in the buffer or wireless bands.

The bidding ended March 30, and the FCC announced the incentive auction was complete on April 12. The auction raised $19.8 billion and made more spectrum available for faster 5G service. Nearly $10.1 billion goes to 175 TV stations, $7.3 billion goes to the United States Treasury, and $1.8 billion is to assist with the repacking process. Lawrence Chu, who was an advisor to the FCC during the bidding, considered the auction a success, while he admitted that "there will be some people disappointed on the broadcaster side."

T-Mobile paid almost $8 billion for 1,525 licenses, which represent 45 percent of low-band spectrum, and this gave the company coverage of the entire country and about four times the spectrum it had before. Dish Network spent $6.2 billion on 486 licenses, and Comcast received 73 licenses for its $1.7 billion bid. AT&T bid $910 million for 23 licenses and U.S. Cellular bid $328.6 million on 188 licenses.

steps.text:
The reverse and forward auctions to repack TV stations and free up spectrum for wireless communications would be carried out in several phases, with targets for how much spectrum would be reallocated, and a balance of payments in which proceeds from the forward auction paid for the reverse auction plus transition costs.

On April 18, 2014, the FCC announced guidelines for the auction. All stations would keep their coverage area as of February 22, 2012, if possible. Channel 37 would become a "guard band" between broadcasting and wireless services. Each station would be given a deadline to make its upgrades, with all stations expected to complete the transition after 39 months. Wheeler later said that stations that could not meet the deadline would not necessarily have to go off the air.[1,2] The FCC approved the framework 3-2, with the NAB claiming the commission had not met its obligation to compensate broadcasters and guarantee service for viewers.[3]

In a July 2, 2015 filing, the Expanding Opportunities for Broadcasters Coalition (EOBC), representing over a hundred TV stations planning to take part in the incentive auction, said that population data was too important and could cause an $8.3 billion drop in opening prices without "relatively minor" changes. Because the incentive auction was a reverse auction, even these prices were the highest possible.[4] On July 16, the FCC planned to finalize the rules of the auction, including requiring stations to move to their new channels 39 months after the auction, and no reserved channel for noncommercial broadcasters.[5] The procedures vote was moved to August 6, but the auction was set for March 29, 2016.[6]

After the vote, FCC commissioner Ajit Pai said the plan "permits too many broadcasters to be placed in the wireless band", resulting in interference between TV stations and others using the band. Dennis Wharton, NAB executive vice president of communications, said the vote minimized what stations would receive for giving up broadcasting, guaranteed numerous interference problems and gave "a handout of free spectrum with no public interest obligations to multibillion dollar companies" while hurting local television news and especially LPTV stations and translators. The LPTV Spectrum Coalition and CTIA objected to the vote, while the EOBC said no one would be happy but the compromise would be enough.[7]

The NAB filed petitions asking the FCC not to penalize stations that did not participate in the auction, and asking that stations not be moved to the duplex gap.[8]

On October 15, the Applications Procedure Public Notice set the filing window as noon December 1 through 6 pm December 18 (later changed to December 8 through January 12). After that, no more stations could join, but bids from those that did would not be final until March 29, 2016. The FCC released opening bid prices on October 16. These fell into three categories: stations giving up or sharing channels (which would mean offering the full price), stations moving from UHF to high VHF (less than full price), and stations moving from high VHF to low VHF (lower than full price but not the lowest). Other factors were the number of people served and interference.[9,10,11]

The FCC designated the auction as Auction 1001, with the purpose of making 144 MHz available for resale to wireless companies. If that target was met, broadcasters would have been repacked into channels up to 26; if the minimum target of 42 MHz was met, channels up to 44 would have been used. If the "clearing target" was not met, a lower target would have been set, with the process continuing until a target was reached.[10] In each market where vacant channels remain, the FCC intends for one of them to be used for unlicensed devices.[12]

The FCC announced that the clearing target would be 126 MHz.[13] This meant fewer channels for relocating LPTV stations, which would not be protected after the auction; thousands of LPTV stations were believed to need relocation.[14] LPTV stations argued that because they were not allowed to participate in the process, they could lose spectrum. On May 5, Scott Caulkins of Caulkins & Bruce PC, representing one of the owners of LPTV stations, argued before the DC Circuit Court that the Spectrum Act and FCC authority gave LPTV stations "essentially the same [spectrum] rights" as full-power stations. He said they could only be considered secondary if they caused interference, but that repacking would result in more interference. FCC attorney Jacob Lewis said LPTV stations would be secondary and that considering their rights would mean too many stations to relocate.[15]

Each bidder in the forward auction had to bid on 95 percent of census blocks in which an interest was shown.[16] As of August, Comcast, AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon and others had submitted bids for 100 MHz of spectrum in the forward auction totaling over $11 billion, against a goal of $88.4 billion.[17]

Only $22.45 billion had been raised when the FCC ended stage one of the forward auction after two weeks.[18] After the second stage of the reverse auction, the target for stage two of the forward auction was 114 MHz, with a desired goal of $54.6 billion,[19] enough for two channels per market. With less spectrum to be purchased, lower demand could mean lower costs for wireless providers. If stage two failed, the target could be reduced further, to 108 MHz, or one channel per market. If stage three also failed, the target could even be 84 MHz, an additional four channels per market. The lower the target, the lower the amount paid to stations, but the fewer the public stations that could participate. And public stations that are not "repacked" must pay for their own equipment upgrades.[20]

Stage two of the forward auction ended October 19 with $21.5 billion in total bids, $33.1 billion less than expected.[21] The third stage of the reverse auction began November 1 with a 108 MHz target. The number of paired blocks per market started at 10, was reduced to 9 in stage two, and to 8 in stage three. Four impaired blocks, with interference in less than 15 percent of an area, protected Mexican channels below 37. Two markets had interference in 15 to 50 percent of an area.[22]

Stage three of the forward auction began December 5 after total bids for stage three came to $40.3 billion for 108 MHz.[23] Stage four of the reverse auction ended January 13, 2017 with $10.05 billion paid for 84 MHz, or seven licenses in each market.[24] Of that, 70 MHz goes to the wireless companies, with 14 MHz for unlicensed use. With less spectrum cleared, fewer stations will move, and none will be in the buffer or wireless bands.[25,26]

Bidding ended March 30,[26] and on April 12 the FCC announced the completion of the incentive auction.[27] The auction raised $19.8 billion and made more spectrum available for faster 5G service. Nearly $10.1 billion goes to 175 TV stations, $7.3 billion to the United States Treasury, and $1.8 billion to help with the repacking process.[28] Lawrence Chu, an advisor to the FCC during the bidding process, considered the auction a success, while admitting that "there will be some people disappointed on the broadcaster side."[29]

T-Mobile paid almost $8 billion for 1,525 licenses representing 45 percent of low-band spectrum, giving the company coverage of the entire country and about four times the spectrum it previously had, while Dish Network spent $6.2 billion on 486 licenses and Comcast received 73 licenses for its $1.7 billion bid. AT&T bid $910 million for 23 licenses and U.S. Cellular bid $328.6 million on 188 licenses.[27,30]
